prompt: A student asks which body tissue shortens to lift the forearm during a biceps curl.

options.text: Muscle tissue specialized for shortening
Epithelial sheets that cover body surfaces
Nervous tissue that conducts electrical signals
Adipose tissue that stores lipid droplets

explanation: Skeletal muscle shortens to lift the forearm, and cardiac and smooth muscle contract in other organs. Epithelium covers surfaces, nervous tissue carries the signal, and adipose stores lipid rather than pulling on bone.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses covering epithelium with muscle, the tissue that actually shortens.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the signal-carrying role of nervous tissue with the contractile tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses energy-storing adipose with muscle, which produces the pull.

prompt: A chart shows a vertical plane passing through the nose, the navel, and the spine. Which portions does that plane separate?

options.text: Upper and lower portions of the body
Left and right portions of the body
Front and back portions of the body
Superficial and deep layers of the skin

explanation: A plane through the nose, navel, and spine is the midsagittal plane, so it separates left from right. A horizontal cut separates superior from inferior, and a frontal cut separates anterior from posterior.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the sagittal plane with the transverse plane, which separates superior from inferior.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the sagittal plane with the frontal plane, which separates anterior from posterior.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a cardinal body plane with the superficial-to-deep layering of skin.

prompt: A client with a freely moving knee asks what structural feature lets the joint surfaces glide on each other.

options.text: Fibrous tissue binding the bones with almost no motion
A fibrocartilage pad joining bones, as at the pubic symphysis
A fluid-filled cavity with cartilage covering the bone ends
A hyaline cartilage plate that later ossifies with growth

explanation: The knee is a synovial joint: synovial fluid fills the cavity, synovial membrane lines the capsule, and articular cartilage covers the bone ends so the surfaces can glide. Fibrous joints barely move, a symphysis uses a fibrocartilage pad, and a growth plate is a synchondrosis.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a synovial joint with a fibrous joint such as a suture, which allows almost no motion.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the knee cavity with a symphysis, where fibrocartilage joins bones without a synovial cavity.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses articular cartilage in a synovial joint with a synchondrosis such as a growth plate.

prompt: A client asks where a normal resting heartbeat begins before the signal reaches the ventricles.

options.text: The atrioventricular node acting as the usual starter
The Purkinje fibers acting as the usual starter
The tricuspid valve leaflets setting the pace
The sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall

explanation: The sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall fires first and sets a normal rhythm. The atrioventricular node delays the impulse, Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricles, and valves direct flow rather than starting the beat.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the sinoatrial node with the atrioventricular node, which delays the impulse rather than starting it.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the pacemaker with Purkinje fibers, which distribute the signal through the ventricular walls.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the electrical pacemaker with the tricuspid valve, which directs blood and does not set rhythm.

prompt: After a long hike, leg muscle cells must restore ATP using oxygen. Which organelle does most of that work?

options.text: Mitochondria, through aerobic respiration
Ribosomes, through assembly of proteins
The Golgi apparatus, through sorting and packaging
Lysosomes, through enzymatic breakdown

explanation: Aerobic ATP production occurs in mitochondria, which is why oxygen-using muscle cells are packed with them. Ribosomes build protein, the Golgi apparatus packages products, and lysosomes digest materials.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses ATP production with ribosomes, whose job is assembling proteins.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses mitochondria with the Golgi apparatus, which sorts and packages cell products.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses energy production with lysosomes, which break materials down by hydrolysis.

prompt: While teaching skin anatomy, the therapist asks which tissue makes up most of the layer just beneath the epidermis.

options.text: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium at the surface
Dense irregular connective tissue with collagen and elastin
Adipose and loose areolar tissue of the subcutaneous layer
Dense regular connective tissue with parallel collagen bundles

explanation: The dermis, just under the epidermis, is mostly dense irregular connective tissue, so collagen runs in many directions. The epidermis is keratinized epithelium, the layer below the dermis is fatty, and parallel collagen is typical of tendons.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the dermis with the epidermis, which is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the dermis with the hypodermis, which is mainly adipose and loose areolar tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses dermal collagen with dense regular tissue, whose parallel bundles are typical of tendons.

prompt: A client with rising blood glucose asks which pancreatic cells release the hormone that lowers it.

options.text: Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
Cortical cells of the adrenal gland
Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
Parafollicular cells of the thyroid

explanation: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets release insulin, which lowers blood glucose. Alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it. The adrenal cortex releases steroid hormones, and thyroid parafollicular cells release calcitonin.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses beta cells with alpha cells, which secrete glucagon and raise blood glucose.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the pancreatic source of insulin with the adrenal cortex, which secretes cortisol and aldosterone.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses insulin-secreting beta cells with thyroid C cells, which secrete calcitonin.

prompt: A therapist asks how the nervous system turns on extra fibers to strengthen a client's grip. Which grouping is activated as one unit?

options.text: A sensory neuron paired with the spindle it monitors
One muscle fiber supplied by several motor neurons
A fascicle of fibers enclosed in perimysium
One motor neuron and the fibers it innervates

explanation: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus the muscle fibers that neuron supplies, and recruiting more units raises grip force. A spindle is a sensory ending, and a fascicle is only a connective-tissue bundle of fibers.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a motor unit with a sensory neuron and the muscle spindle it monitors.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the motor unit: one motor neuron supplies many fibers, and each fiber receives one neuron.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a motor unit with a fascicle, which is a bundle of fibers wrapped in perimysium.

prompt: Interstitial fluid that blood capillaries leave behind in the lower leg must get back toward the blood. Which vessels do that job?

options.text: Lymph vessels that return interstitial fluid to blood
Arteries carrying oxygenated blood out to capillary beds
Veins returning deoxygenated blood to the right atrium
Portal vessels carrying sugars from the gut to the liver

explanation: Lymphatic capillaries collect interstitial fluid that blood capillaries leave behind and return it toward the venous blood. Arteries deliver blood outward, veins return blood itself, and the hepatic portal route carries absorbed nutrients.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses lymphatics with arteries, which carry blood out toward capillary beds.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses lymph return of interstitial fluid with veins, which return blood to the right atrium.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses lymph vessels with the hepatic portal route, which carries absorbed sugars to the liver.

prompt: Sweating and widening skin vessels bring an elevated body temperature back toward its usual range. What is that stability called?

options.text: Positive feedback that amplifies a change to an endpoint
Homeostasis, a relatively stable internal environment
Catabolism, the breakdown of molecules for energy
Metabolism, the sum of the body's chemical reactions

explanation: Pulling body temperature back toward its usual range is homeostasis, typically through negative feedback. Positive feedback amplifies a change until an endpoint. Catabolism and metabolism describe chemical reactions, not that stable internal condition.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses homeostasis with positive feedback, which amplifies a change until a process ends.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses homeostasis with catabolism, the breakdown of molecules to release energy.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses homeostasis with metabolism, the sum of the body's chemical reactions.

prompt: A client curls a light dumbbell, bending the elbow to bring the hand toward the shoulder. Which muscles do most of that bend?

options.text: Triceps brachii working together with anconeus
Biceps brachii working together with brachialis
Coracobrachialis working together with the deltoid
Pronator teres working together with supinator

explanation: Elbow flexion in a curl is produced mainly by brachialis and biceps brachii. Triceps brachii and anconeus extend the elbow. Coracobrachialis and the anterior deltoid move the shoulder, and pronator teres and supinator rotate the forearm.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses elbow flexors with triceps brachii and anconeus, which extend the elbow.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses elbow flexion with coracobrachialis and deltoid, which flex the shoulder.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the elbow flexors with pronator teres and supinator, which rotate the forearm.

prompt: Five days after a calf strain, the healing tissue is pink and filled with new capillaries and fibroblasts. Which stage is this?

options.text: The inflammatory stage, dominated by clotting and neutrophils
The proliferative stage, forming granulation tissue
The remodeling stage, when collagen aligns to load
The hemostasis stage, limited to forming the clot

explanation: New capillaries and fibroblasts a few days after injury form granulation tissue, which marks the proliferative stage. Clotting and neutrophil influx come first, and collagen realignment is the later remodeling stage.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses day-five granulation tissue with the earlier inflammatory stage of clotting and neutrophils.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses granulation tissue with remodeling, the later stage when collagen realigns to load.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a vascular healing bed with hemostasis, the brief first stage of clot formation.

prompt: A client training for a hike asks which organ system brings oxygen in and lets carbon dioxide leave the blood.

options.text: The digestive system, by absorbing nutrients from food
The respiratory system, by exchanging gases in the lungs
The integumentary system, by managing heat loss through skin
The lymphatic system, by returning fluid from the tissues

explanation: Moving oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out is pulmonary gas exchange, the work of the respiratory system. Digestion absorbs nutrients, skin is a barrier and heat regulator, and lymphatics return fluid.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses gas exchange with the digestive system, which absorbs nutrients from food.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the lungs with the integumentary system, whose main roles are barrier and heat loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses pulmonary gas exchange with the lymphatic system, which returns interstitial fluid.

prompt: An instructor slices a torso model horizontally, parallel to the floor, at the level of the navel. Which portions does that slice separate?

options.text: Left and right portions of the body
Superior and inferior portions of the body
Anterior and posterior portions of the body
Proximal and distal portions along a limb

explanation: A horizontal slice parallel to the floor is a transverse plane, so it separates superior from inferior portions. Left-right separation is sagittal, and front-back separation is frontal. Proximal and distal are limb position terms.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the transverse plane with the sagittal plane, which separates left from right.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the transverse plane with the frontal plane, which separates anterior from posterior.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a body plane with proximal and distal, which locate sites along a limb.

prompt: A client points to the cord running from the calf muscle into the heel bone and asks what that cord is.

options.text: A ligament joining one bone directly to another bone
A tendon joining that muscle to the heel bone
A bursa, a fluid-filled sac that cushions nearby tissue
Periosteum, the membrane covering the bone surface

explanation: The cord from the calf muscle to the calcaneus is the calcaneal tendon. Tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone, a bursa is a nearby fluid-filled sac, and periosteum covers the bone itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a tendon, which joins muscle to bone, with a ligament, which joins bone to bone.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the cordlike tendon with a bursa, the fluid-filled sac that reduces friction beside it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the tendon with periosteum, the membrane that covers the bone surface.

prompt: Minutes after an ankle sprain, the area is red, warm, and swollen as vessels dilate and immune cells arrive. Which phase is underway?

options.text: Inflammation, with dilated vessels and immune cells
Proliferation, with granulation tissue filling the gap
Remodeling, with collagen fibers aligning to stress
Callus formation, as in the repair of a fracture

explanation: Redness, heat, and swelling within minutes are the inflammatory phase: local vessels dilate and immune cells enter. Granulation and collagen remodeling come later. A fracture callus is bone repair, not the first response of a sprain.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses immediate redness and swelling with proliferation, when granulation tissue fills the wound later.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the first inflammatory response with remodeling, when collagen later aligns to stress.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses soft-tissue inflammation of a sprain with callus formation in fracture repair.

prompt: Wavelike mixing in the small intestine continues without the client deciding to contract it. Which muscle tissue produces that motion?

options.text: Smooth muscle in the wall of the intestine
Skeletal muscle under voluntary control
Cardiac muscle with branching fibers in the heart
Dense connective tissue of the supporting mesentery

explanation: Mixing and peristalsis in the intestine come from smooth muscle in the wall, which contracts without a conscious decision. Skeletal muscle is voluntary, cardiac muscle forms the heart, and the mesentery is connective tissue.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses involuntary gut motion with skeletal muscle, which is under voluntary control.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses smooth muscle of the gut with cardiac muscle, the branching muscle of the heart.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the contracting wall with the mesentery, which is connective tissue that supports the gut.

prompt: Deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior vena cava arrives at the heart. Which chamber receives that blood first?

options.text: The right atrium, before the right ventricle
The left atrium, receiving blood from the lungs
The left ventricle, just before the aorta
The right ventricle, before the pulmonary trunk

explanation: Blood in the venae cavae enters the right atrium first, then the right ventricle, then the lungs. The left atrium receives blood returning from the lungs, and the left ventricle ejects into the aorta.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses vena-cava return with the left atrium, which receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the receiving chamber with the left ventricle, which pumps into the aorta.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the right atrium with the right ventricle, which is the next chamber, not the first.

prompt: Laboratory results show a low blood calcium level, and calcium begins to leave bone. Which hormone drives that release?

options.text: Parathyroid hormone from the parathyroid glands
Calcitonin from the thyroid parafollicular cells
Insulin from the beta cells of the pancreas
Aldosterone from the cortex of the adrenal gland

explanation: Parathyroid hormone raises a low blood calcium level, in part by driving release of calcium from bone. Calcitonin lowers blood calcium. Insulin acts on glucose, and aldosterone acts on sodium and potassium.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses parathyroid hormone with calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium rather than raising it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses calcium regulation with insulin, which lowers blood glucose.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses parathyroid hormone with aldosterone, which regulates sodium and potassium balance.

prompt: During a breathing lesson, the therapist explains where inhaled oxygen actually crosses into the pulmonary blood.

options.text: Thin-walled alveoli surrounded by capillaries
The trachea, before air reaches either bronchus
The pleural cavity between the lung and the chest wall
The nasal cavity, where incoming air is warmed and filtered

explanation: Inhaled oxygen enters the blood across the thin walls of alveoli and the capillaries wrapped around them. The trachea and nose conduct and condition air. The pleural cavity is the space around the lung, not the exchange surface.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the alveoli with the trachea, which conducts air and is not the exchange surface.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses alveolar exchange with the pleural cavity, the potential space around the lung.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses gas exchange with the nasal cavity, which warms and filters incoming air.

prompt: A nerve impulse jumps between gaps along a peripheral axon and arrives quickly at a muscle. What covering makes that speed possible?

options.text: Endoneurium wrapping one axon in loose tissue
Epineurium binding the whole nerve into one trunk
A myelin sheath produced by Schwann cells
Perineurium bundling groups of axons into fascicles

explanation: Myelin from Schwann cells insulates a peripheral axon so the impulse jumps from node to node. Endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium are connective-tissue wrappings; they organize the nerve but do not create that saltatory speed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the myelin sheath with endoneurium, the loose connective tissue around a single axon.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses myelin with epineurium, the outer wrapping of the whole nerve trunk.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses myelin with perineurium, which bundles axons into a fascicle.

prompt: As a healed fracture is reshaped, old bone matrix is dissolved so the bone can match its new load. Which cells dissolve that matrix?

options.text: Osteoblasts, which deposit new bone matrix
Osteocytes, which reside in mature lacunae
Osteoclasts, which resorb mineralized matrix
Chondrocytes, which maintain cartilage matrix

explanation: Osteoclasts break down mineralized matrix when reshaping bone releases or removes old tissue. Osteoblasts lay down new matrix, osteocytes maintain bone from inside lacunae, and chondrocytes belong to cartilage.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses osteoclasts, which resorb bone, with osteoblasts, which deposit new matrix.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses osteoclasts with osteocytes, the mature cells that maintain bone from lacunae.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses bone-resorbing osteoclasts with chondrocytes, which maintain cartilage.

prompt: After a long hot session without enough water, urine becomes scant and concentrated. Which hormone told the kidneys to reabsorb more water?

options.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide released from the heart atria
Aldosterone secreted by the adrenal cortex
Antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary
Cortisol released by the adrenal cortex in stress

explanation: Antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary adds water channels in the collecting ducts, so urine becomes scant and concentrated. Aldosterone saves sodium. Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes loss of sodium and water. Cortisol is a stress steroid.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses antidiuretic hormone with atrial natriuretic peptide, which promotes sodium and water loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses water-channel retention with aldosterone, whose direct renal effect is sodium reabsorption.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses antidiuretic hormone with cortisol, a stress steroid from the adrenal cortex.

prompt: An adult needs new red blood cells after several weeks of heavy training. Where are most of those cells formed?

options.text: Yellow marrow, which stores fat inside long bones
The spleen, treated as the main adult production site
Red bone marrow within spaces of spongy bone
The liver, which forms most blood cells in an adult

explanation: In an adult, most new blood cells form in red bone marrow inside spongy bone. Yellow marrow is mostly stored fat. The liver and spleen matter in fetal life or when marrow cannot keep up, not as the usual adult site.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses red marrow, where blood cells form, with yellow marrow, which is mostly fat.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses adult red marrow with the spleen, which is not the main site of blood-cell formation after birth.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses adult red marrow with the liver, a major site of blood-cell formation before birth.

prompt: A skeletal muscle fiber shortens when thin filaments slide toward the center of each contractile unit. Which proteins do that sliding?

options.text: Collagen and elastin in the surrounding fascia
Keratin and melanin in the overlying epidermis
Actin and myosin inside each sarcomere
Troponin and tropomyosin acting as the filaments themselves

explanation: A fiber shortens when actin thin filaments slide past myosin thick filaments within each sarcomere. Collagen and elastin are connective-tissue fibers, keratin and melanin are skin products, and troponin and tropomyosin regulate binding rather than forming the sliding pair.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses contractile filaments with collagen and elastin in the fascia around the muscle.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses actin and myosin with keratin and melanin, which are products of the skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the sliding filaments with troponin and tropomyosin, which regulate myosin binding.

prompt: Lymph drained from a swollen foot passes through small bean-shaped organs before it returns toward the veins. What is the main job of those organs?

options.text: Pump oxygenated blood outward toward the leg muscles
Secrete digestive enzymes into the passing lymph
Store bile until a meal reaches the small intestine
Filter lymph and house cells of the immune response

explanation: Those bean-shaped organs are lymph nodes. They filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages that respond to debris and microbes. They do not pump arterial blood, secrete digestive enzymes, or store bile.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses lymph nodes with arteries, which carry oxygenated blood out to the leg.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses lymph-node filtering with secretion of digestive enzymes, which is a job of digestive glands.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses lymph nodes with the gallbladder, which stores bile.

prompt: The muscular wall of the heart needs its own oxygen supply while a client walks briskly to the clinic. Which vessels provide that blood?

options.text: Pulmonary veins bringing blood back from the lungs
The superior vena cava returning blood from the head and arms
Hepatic portal veins carrying blood from the digestive organs
Coronary arteries branching from the ascending aorta

explanation: Heart muscle receives its own blood from the coronary arteries, which leave the ascending aorta. Pulmonary veins return lung blood to the left atrium, the superior vena cava returns systemic blood to the right atrium, and the hepatic portal vein serves the liver.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the coronary supply of heart muscle with pulmonary veins, which return blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coronary arteries with the superior vena cava, which returns systemic blood to the right atrium.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coronary arteries with the hepatic portal vein, which carries blood from digestive organs to the liver.

prompt: Months after a shoulder scar forms, collagen fibers slowly realign along the lines of stress. Which healing phase is that?

options.text: Early inflammation, while the area is still red and puffy
Clot formation, finished long before the scar looks settled
Granulation, when new vessels first fill the open wound
Remodeling, as collagen realigns with mechanical stress

explanation: Months later, collagen reorganizing along lines of stress is the remodeling phase. Inflammation is the early red swollen stage, clot formation is hemostasis, and granulation belongs to proliferation while the wound is still filling in.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses late collagen realignment with inflammation, the early stage of redness and swelling.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses remodeling with hemostasis, the clot that forms at the start of healing.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses remodeling with granulation, which fills the wound during proliferation.

prompt: A nervous client shows a faster pulse, wider pupils, and sweaty palms just before the session starts. Which autonomic division is dominant?

options.text: The parasympathetic division, which slows the heart and supports rest
The somatic motor division, which contracts skeletal muscle
The enteric division, which coordinates motility in the gut
The sympathetic division preparing the body for stress

explanation: A faster pulse, wider pupils, and sweaty palms are sympathetic effects that prepare the body for stress. The parasympathetic division slows the heart during rest, somatic neurons move skeletal muscle, and the enteric division runs the gut.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the stress response with the parasympathetic division, which slows the heart and supports rest.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an autonomic stress pattern with the somatic motor division, which contracts skeletal muscle.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the sympathetic stress response with the enteric division, which coordinates gut motility.

prompt: The first step in forming urine pushes water and small solutes out of a capillary tuft into a surrounding capsule. Where does that step occur?

options.text: The loop of Henle, where the medullary gradient is built
The distal tubule, a major site of aldosterone action
The collecting duct, where water can be reclaimed later
Glomerular capillaries inside Bowman's capsule

explanation: Urine formation starts when glomerular capillaries filter water and small solutes into Bowman's capsule. The loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient, the distal tubule responds strongly to aldosterone, and the collecting duct can reclaim water later.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the filtration step with the loop of Henle, which builds the medullary concentration gradient.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses glomerular filtration with the distal tubule, a major site of aldosterone-sensitive sodium handling.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the first filtration step with the collecting duct, where water reabsorption can occur later.

prompt: During a seated curl, a client asks which muscle does most of the work as the elbow bends and the dumbbell rises toward the shoulder. Which role is the biceps brachii filling?

options.text: Prime mover producing most of the force that flexes the elbow
Opposing muscle that lengthens on the back of the arm as the elbow bends
Helper that adds a smaller share of force but does not lead the curl
Stabilizer that pins the scapula in place so the elbow is free to bend

explanation: The agonist, also called the prime mover, is the muscle mainly responsible for the joint action being performed. In a curl, biceps brachii produces the elbow-flexion torque, so it is the agonist rather than a muscle that opposes, assists, or merely steadies the scapula.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the agonist with the antagonist, which lengthens and opposes elbow flexion during the curl.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the agonist with a synergist, which assists the prime mover but does not supply most of the force.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the agonist with a fixator, which stabilizes a proximal bone so the movement can occur.

prompt: A client presses both palms together at chest height and holds the effort while the elbows stay at one angle and the hands do not travel. Which contraction are the pressing muscles using?

options.text: The muscle shortens and the elbows move as tension overcomes the press
Tension builds while muscle length and the elbow angle stay fixed
The muscle lengthens as an outside load pulls the hands apart
The hands travel through the press at one machine-set constant speed

explanation: An isometric contraction develops tension without a change in muscle length or joint angle. Pressing the palms together and holding still meets that definition because the elbows do not move while the muscles work.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an isometric hold with a concentric contraction, in which the muscle shortens and the joint moves.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an isometric hold with an eccentric contraction, in which the muscle lengthens under an external load.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an isometric hold with isokinetic exercise, in which a device keeps the speed constant.

prompt: During a range screen the client bends the elbow so the forearm travels toward the upper arm. Which joint action is that?

options.text: Extension, which increases the angle between the humerus and the forearm
Abduction, which carries a limb farther from the midline of the body
Flexion, which decreases the angle between the bones at that joint
Pronation, which rotates the forearm so the palm turns toward the floor

explanation: Flexion is the action that decreases the angle between bones at a joint. Drawing the forearm toward the upper arm closes the elbow, so the motion is flexion. Extension opens the angle, and abduction and pronation are different actions.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses flexion with extension, the opposite action, which increases the joint angle.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses flexion with abduction, which moves a limb away from the midline.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses flexion with pronation, a forearm rotation that turns the palm posteriorly.

prompt: On a side-view posture check, the client's low back arches deeply inward, the abdomen tips forward, and the lumbar curve looks increased. Which spinal term matches that shape?

options.text: Scoliosis, a lateral curve of the thoracic or lumbar column with rotation
Kyphosis, an exaggerated posterior curve of the thoracic region
Flat-back posture, with loss of the normal anterior lumbar curve
Lordosis, an exaggerated anterior curve of the lumbar spine

explanation: Lordosis is an exaggerated anterior spinal curve, most often noted in the lumbar region when the low back arches inward and the abdomen shifts forward. A lateral curve is scoliosis, and an increased thoracic posterior curve is kyphosis.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses lordosis with scoliosis, which is a lateral spinal curve rather than an anterior one.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses lordosis with kyphosis, the increased posterior curvature of the thoracic spine.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an increased lumbar curve with flat back, which reduces that curve.

prompt: A data-entry worker reports nighttime numbness in the thumb, index finger, and middle finger that flares when the wrist stays flexed. The compression site is at the wrist. Which nerve is trapped?

options.text: Median nerve where it passes under the flexor retinaculum
Ulnar nerve where it passes through Guyon's canal at the wrist
Radial nerve where it is compressed in the radial tunnel
Median nerve where pronator teres compresses it near the elbow

explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist, which matches numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers provoked by sustained wrist flexion. Ulnar, radial, and elbow-level median entrapments produce different patterns.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses carpal tunnel with ulnar compression in Guyon's canal, which affects the ring and little fingers.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses carpal tunnel with radial tunnel syndrome, a radial-nerve entrapment near the elbow.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses carpal tunnel with pronator teres syndrome, which entraps the median nerve at the elbow.

prompt: A client in their fifties describes a gradual shoulder ache that became a global loss of motion. Passive flexion, abduction, and external rotation are limited, and external rotation is the most restricted. Which condition fits?

options.text: Subacromial bursitis with a painful arc but passive motion still available at end range
Adhesive capsulitis with a progressively stiff shoulder capsule
Biceps tendinopathy felt mainly when the elbow flexes against resistance
Glenohumeral instability with capsular laxity and excess passive motion

explanation: Adhesive capsulitis tightens the glenohumeral capsule and limits passive motion in a capsular pattern, with external rotation often lost the most. A painful arc with preserved passive range, isolated biceps pain, or a lax capsule point to other shoulder problems.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses frozen shoulder with subacromial bursitis, which tends to limit a painful arc while passive range remains more available.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a capsular pattern with biceps tendinopathy, a contractile problem felt when the elbow works against resistance.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses capsular stiffness with instability, which increases passive motion instead of restricting it.

prompt: A runner's Achilles tendon is warm, swollen, and locally sore two days after a sharp increase in hill repeats. The note uses the acute inflammatory tendon term, separate from the degenerative one. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Tendinitis means a degenerative tendon, and tendinosis means inflammation of that tendon
Tendinitis names sheath inflammation, and tendinosis names a partial tendon tear
Tendinitis means an inflamed tendon, and tendinosis means degeneration
Tendinitis names bursal inflammation, and tendinosis names tendon degeneration

explanation: In exam usage, tendinitis means an acutely inflamed tendon, while tendinosis means degenerative tendon change without that inflammatory picture. Warmth and swelling after a sudden workload fit the inflammatory term. Everyday practice often groups both under tendinopathy.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the pair, calling tendinitis degenerative and tendinosis inflammatory.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses tendinitis with tenosynovitis of the sheath, and treats tendinosis as if it were a tear.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses tendinitis with bursitis, which is inflammation of a bursa rather than of the tendon.

prompt: The iliotibial (IT) band can contribute to lateral knee pain associated with:

options.text: Patellofemoral pain syndrome around the anterior kneecap
Pes anserine bursitis at the medial proximal tibia
Patellar tendinopathy at the inferior pole of the kneecap in jumpers
IT band friction syndrome near the lateral femoral epicondyle

explanation: Repetitive flexion/extension can irritate tissues under the IT band at the lateral knee.

distractorExplanations.a: Patellofemoral pain is felt around the front of the kneecap, not at the lateral femoral epicondyle under the IT band.
distractorExplanations.b: Pes anserine bursitis causes medial knee pain at the proximal tibia, not lateral IT band pain.
distractorExplanations.c: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) causes anterior pain below the kneecap, not lateral knee pain.

prompt: A sprinter feels a sudden pull in the posterior thigh, then has pain and weakness when the hamstring contracts. Ligament tests show no joint laxity. Which injury fits?

options.text: Strain of the hamstring muscle or the tendon that joins it to bone
Sprain of a ligament that normally restrains excess knee motion
Contusion from a direct impact that bruises muscle without a tensile tear
Delayed-onset soreness that appears a day after an unfamiliar workout

explanation: A strain is an injury of muscle or tendon, typically a sudden tensile pull with pain when that muscle contracts. A sprain damages a ligament and is more likely to create joint laxity, which this sprinter does not have.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a strain with a sprain, which injures a ligament rather than the muscle-tendon unit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a tensile strain with a contusion, which is bruising from a direct blow.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an acute strain with delayed-onset muscle soreness, which builds later and lacks a sudden tear.

prompt: With the eyes closed, a client can tell that the elbow was moved into flexion and can copy that angle with the other arm. Which receptors provide that position sense?

options.text: Nociceptors, which report actual or threatened tissue damage as pain
Proprioceptors, which report position and movement of the limb
Thermoreceptors, which report warming and cooling at the skin surface
Baroreceptors, which report increases and decreases in blood pressure

explanation: Proprioceptors such as muscle spindles and joint receptors supply the sense of position and movement, which is why a client can match an elbow angle without looking. Pain, skin temperature, and blood pressure are reported by other receptor types.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses proprioceptors with nociceptors, which signal painful or tissue-damaging stimuli.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses proprioceptors with thermoreceptors, which detect temperature change in the skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses proprioceptors with baroreceptors, which monitor arterial blood pressure.

prompt: While lowering a grocery bag from a high shelf, the client slowly straightens the elbow and the biceps controls the descent. Which contraction is the biceps doing?

options.text: Concentric work, in which the biceps shortens to lift the bag higher
Eccentric work, in which the biceps lengthens while staying active
Isometric work, in which biceps tension rises with the elbow held still
Isokinetic work, in which a device forces the elbow to one fixed speed

explanation: An eccentric contraction generates tension while the muscle lengthens. The biceps controls the bag on the way down, staying active as the elbow extends and the muscle gets longer. It is not shortening, holding a fixed length, or moving at a machine-set speed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses this controlled lowering with a concentric contraction, in which the biceps would shorten to raise the bag.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses eccentric lowering with an isometric contraction, which holds tension without a change in length.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses eccentric muscle action with isokinetic exercise, which is defined by constant speed on a device.

prompt: The client lifts one arm straight out to the side in the frontal plane until the hand is level with the shoulder, taking the limb away from the trunk. Which glenohumeral action is that?

options.text: Adduction, drawing that arm back in toward the side of the trunk
Abduction, carrying that arm away from the midline of the body
Flexion, swinging the arm forward and up in the sagittal plane
Lateral rotation, turning the humerus outward in the glenoid

explanation: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline in the frontal plane, which is what happens when the arm is lifted out to the side. Adduction returns it toward the trunk, flexion travels in the sagittal plane, and lateral rotation spins the humerus.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses abduction with adduction, the action that brings the arm back toward the midline.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses frontal-plane abduction with flexion, which moves the arm in the sagittal plane.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses abduction with lateral rotation, which turns the humerus in the socket rather than lifting it away from the trunk.

prompt: During the upward phase of a push-up, the triceps straighten the elbows. Which role does the biceps on the front of the arm play?

options.text: Prime mover creating most of the torque that extends the elbow
Antagonist that yields and lengthens during elbow extension
Synergist assisting the triceps as they extend the elbow joint
Fixator steadying the scapula so the push-up can be completed

explanation: The antagonist opposes the action in progress and lengthens while the prime mover shortens. On the way up from a push-up the triceps extend the elbow, so biceps brachii, an elbow flexor, is the antagonist and must lengthen to let the elbow straighten.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the antagonist with the agonist. The triceps, rather than the lengthening biceps, is the prime mover of elbow extension here.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the antagonist with a synergist, which would assist the triceps instead of opposing elbow extension.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the antagonist with a fixator, which stabilizes a proximal segment rather than opposing the motion.

prompt: A client rises from a squat with both feet planted, so the feet stay fixed on the floor while the knees and hips extend. How should that movement be classified?

options.text: Open chain, because the foot would be free to move through the air
Closed chain, because the distal foot stays fixed on the floor
Isometric, because the muscle length would stay constant throughout
Isokinetic, because a dynamometer would hold the speed constant

explanation: A closed-chain movement keeps the distal segment fixed while the rest of the limb moves over it. A squat does that: the feet stay on the floor. A seated leg extension, where the foot moves freely, is open chain. Contraction type is a separate classification.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses closed chain with open chain, in which the distal segment moves freely in space.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a kinetic-chain category with an isometric contraction, which describes constant muscle length.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses closed-chain exercise with isokinetic work, which is defined by a constant speed on a device.

prompt: A client who spends the day hunched over a laptop presents with a rounded upper back and shoulders rolled forward. Which term names that curve?

options.text: Lordosis, an excessive forward curve of the lumbar spine
Kyphosis, an excessive backward curve of the thoracic spine
Scoliosis, a lateral spinal curve combined with vertebral rotation
Spondylolisthesis, forward slippage of one vertebra on the vertebra below

explanation: Kyphosis is an exaggerated posterior curvature, classically of the thoracic spine, and it shows up as a rounded upper back. It is distinct from lumbar lordosis, from a lateral scoliotic curve, and from spondylolisthesis, which is a vertebral slip rather than a curve.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses kyphosis with lordosis, the increased anterior curve usually described in the lumbar spine.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses kyphosis with scoliosis, a side-bending curve that also involves rotation of the vertebrae.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a spinal curve with spondylolisthesis, which is anterior translation of one vertebra on another.

prompt: A client points to the front of the neck beside the windpipe and asks for deep thumb work on the scalenes, directly over a clearly felt carotid pulse. What is the safe decision?

options.text: Refuse deep pressure on the anterior neck and work posterior tissues
Glide firmly along the carotid pulse because the scalenes feel tight there
Pin the anterior scalene hard against the cervical transverse processes
Compress the pulse point for a full minute to quiet a scalene trigger

explanation: The anterior neck is an endangerment site because the carotid artery, jugular vein, vagus nerve, and trachea lie close to the surface. Deep pressure over the carotid pulse is unsafe. Posterior neck and shoulder work can address tension without compressing those structures.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a request for scalene work with permission to glide deeply along the carotid artery, an endangerment site.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses careful scalene contact with deep pinning on the anterior neck, which risks vessels and nerves.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses trigger-point compression with a safe technique when the contact is directly over the carotid pulse.

prompt: While stroking the hamstrings, the therapist's thumb sinks into the soft hollow behind the client's slightly flexed knee, where the popliteal pulse is palpable. What should the therapist do?

options.text: Shift contact onto the hamstring belly and stay out of that hollow
Press deeper in the hollow to reach the posterior capsule of the knee
Strip lengthwise through the hollow along the popliteal vessels
Hold a trigger-point press in the hollow until the foot tingles

explanation: The popliteal fossa is an endangerment site containing the popliteal artery and vein and the tibial nerve. Deep or pointed pressure there can compromise those structures. The hamstring muscle belly can be treated without entering the hollow behind the knee.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses access to the posterior capsule with a license for deep pressure in the popliteal fossa.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a longitudinal stroke with a safe path when the stroke follows the popliteal vessels.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a trigger-point hold with safe work when the pressure sits on the popliteal neurovascular bundle.

prompt: Before any leg work, the client reports that one calf swelled, reddened, and turned warm overnight after a long flight, and light touch on that calf is painful. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Stop the session and refer the client for urgent medical evaluation
Use deep calf stripping in the hope of breaking up a suspected clot
Apply vigorous petrissage to the warm calf to push the swelling out
Stretch the calf firmly today and recheck the swelling next session

explanation: Sudden unilateral calf swelling, warmth, redness, and tenderness after prolonged sitting are warning signs of acute deep-vein thrombosis. Massage, deep stripping, and stretching are contraindicated because they may dislodge a clot. The session stops and the client needs urgent medical care.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a possible thrombus with tissue that can be safely stripped, which risks breaking a clot loose.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses acute swelling from a possible clot with ordinary edema that petrissage might move.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an urgent vascular warning with muscle tightness that can wait for the next visit.

prompt: A client arrives flushed and sweaty, says a fever began yesterday, and reports an ache through the whole body, but still wants a full-body massage today. What is the appropriate plan?

options.text: Reschedule the session and wait until the fever resolves
Give a shorter session that still uses fast circulatory strokes
Work the feet and skip massage for the rest of the body
Apply hot packs across the back to help sweat the fever out

explanation: Fever with a body-wide ache is a systemic contraindication. Massage increases circulation and is not appropriate while the client is febrile, including a shortened session, foot work, or added heat. The safe plan is to postpone until the fever has resolved.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a shorter appointment with a safe modification. Fever is a systemic reason to postpone, not a reason to speed up the strokes.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses foot work with a way around a systemic contraindication. Fever affects the whole client, not one region.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses heat and sweating with treatment for fever. Added heat is inappropriate while the client is febrile.

prompt: A quick tap on the patellar tendon makes the quadriceps jerk into a short contraction. The therapist links that jerk to a stretch-sensitive receptor lying inside the muscle. Which receptor is it?

options.text: Muscle spindle, which senses a quick stretch and triggers contraction
Golgi tendon organ, which senses heavy tension and then inhibits the muscle
Pacinian corpuscle, which senses vibration and rapid pressure change
Meissner corpuscle, which senses light touch on hairless skin

explanation: Muscle spindles sit in the muscle belly and respond to stretch by facilitating contraction, which is the basis of the stretch reflex seen in a tendon tap. Golgi tendon organs respond to tension by inhibiting the muscle, and the skin corpuscles do not drive this jerk.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the muscle spindle with the Golgi tendon organ, which responds to tendon tension by inhibiting contraction.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the muscle spindle with a Pacinian corpuscle, a skin receptor for vibration and pressure change.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the muscle spindle with a Meissner corpuscle, a skin receptor for light touch.

prompt: After the client presses the heel hard into the table for several seconds, the hamstring suddenly lengthens more easily. Which receptor accounts for that ease?

options.text: Muscle spindle, which responds when muscle fibers are stretched quickly
Ruffini ending, which reports slow stretch in the skin and joint capsule
Golgi tendon organ, which monitors high tension in the tendon
Krause end bulb, a skin receptor tied mainly to sensing cold

explanation: The Golgi tendon organ monitors tension where muscle fibers meet tendon. When tension is high, it inhibits that muscle, the autogenic effect used to explain why a strong contraction is followed by easier lengthening. The muscle spindle responds to stretch, not to this tension-driven ease.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the Golgi tendon organ with the muscle spindle, which responds to stretch by facilitating contraction.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the Golgi tendon organ with a Ruffini ending, a receptor for slow skin and joint stretch.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the Golgi tendon organ with a Krause end bulb, which is associated with cold sensation.

prompt: From a fully straightened elbow, the client curls a water bottle up to the shoulder and the biceps bunches under the load. Which contraction is the biceps using?

options.text: Eccentric action, because the biceps would be lengthening under the load
Isometric action, because the elbow angle would stay fixed during the lift
Concentric action, because the biceps shortens as it lifts
Isokinetic action, because equipment would be locking the lifting speed

explanation: A concentric contraction shortens the muscle as it overcomes the load. Curling the bottle up into elbow flexion shortens the biceps, so the contraction is concentric. Lengthening, a static hold, and machine-controlled speed describe other contraction types.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the lifting phase with an eccentric contraction, in which the biceps would lengthen while controlling the bottle downward.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a moving lift with an isometric contraction, which produces tension without a change in joint angle.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a free lift with isokinetic exercise, which requires a device to keep the speed constant.

prompt: A client can keep the arm out to the side once it is already raised, but struggles to begin that lift through the first few degrees off the thigh. Which muscle normally starts that early motion?

options.text: Latissimus dorsi, which adducts, extends, and medially rotates the humerus
Pectoralis major, which flexes and adducts the humerus across the chest
Supraspinatus, which initiates abduction at the glenohumeral joint
Teres major, which adducts and medially rotates the humerus

explanation: Supraspinatus initiates glenohumeral abduction through the first roughly 15 degrees, after which the deltoid becomes the main abductor. Difficulty starting the arm off the side, with the ability to hold it once raised, points to that initiation role. The other muscles listed adduct or flex rather than start abduction.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the abductor that starts the lift with latissimus dorsi, a powerful adductor and extensor.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses supraspinatus with pectoralis major, which flexes and adducts the humerus.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses supraspinatus with teres major, an adductor and medial rotator, not an abductor.

prompt: Rising from a low chair, the client drives the hips from a deeply flexed position into extension against full body weight. Which muscle is the primary hip extensor for that effort?

options.text: Iliopsoas, which flexes the hip and can pull the lumbar spine forward
Gluteus medius, which abducts the hip and steadies the pelvis in gait
Gluteus maximus, which extends the hip against a heavy load
Tensor fasciae latae, which flexes and abducts the hip at the same time

explanation: Gluteus maximus is the primary hip extensor when the hip starts in flexion and the load is high, as in standing up from a low chair. Iliopsoas and tensor fasciae latae flex the hip, and gluteus medius abducts it, so they do not drive this extension.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the hip extensor with iliopsoas, the primary hip flexor.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses gluteus maximus with gluteus medius, which abducts the hip and stabilizes the pelvis.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses gluteus maximus with tensor fasciae latae, which flexes and abducts the hip.

prompt: The client lets the arm stay limp while the therapist raises it into shoulder flexion until a firm end feel stops the motion. The client adds no muscular effort. Which range was measured?

options.text: Active range, produced entirely by the client's own muscle contraction
Active-assisted range, produced jointly by the client and the therapist
Passive range, moved by the therapist while the client relaxes
Resistive range, produced as the client pushes back against a load

explanation: Passive range of motion is movement produced by an outside force, here the therapist, while the client remains relaxed. Active range requires the client's own contraction, and active-assisted range splits the effort. A firm end feel marks the end of the available passive motion.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses passive motion with active range, which the client would have to produce by contracting.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses passive motion with active-assisted range, in which the client still contributes some effort.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a relaxed passive test with resistive testing, in which the client pushes against a load.

prompt: As the client reaches overhead for a high shelf, the lower tip of the shoulder blade swings out toward the side. Which scapular motion is occurring?

options.text: Downward rotation, tilting the glenoid cavity toward the feet
Retraction, sliding the scapula medially toward the vertebral column
Upward rotation, tilting the glenoid cavity toward the head
Depression, drawing the whole scapula down toward the pelvis

explanation: Overhead reaching requires upward rotation of the scapula: the inferior angle moves laterally and the glenoid faces upward. That motion is produced by the trapezius and serratus anterior force couple. Downward rotation, retraction, and depression orient or place the scapula differently.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses upward rotation with downward rotation, which tips the glenoid toward the feet.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses upward rotation with retraction, a medial slide of the scapula toward the spine.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses upward rotation with depression, which lowers the scapula rather than turning the glenoid up.

prompt: Against light resistance, the client turns the face to the left, and the sternocleidomastoid on the right side of the neck stands out. What is that right muscle doing?

options.text: Turning the face toward the same side as the muscle that is contracting
Extending the neck so the chin lifts straight toward the ceiling
Drawing the scapulae back and pulling both clavicles posteriorly
Turning the face toward the side opposite the contracting muscle

explanation: Acting on one side, sternocleidomastoid rotates the head to the opposite side and sidebends the neck to the same side. A prominent right sternocleidomastoid while the face turns left is that contralateral rotation. Same-side rotation, a chin lift, and scapular retraction are different actions.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the rotation. One sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side, not the same side.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses unilateral rotation with lifting the chin. The tested action is turning the face to the opposite side.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses sternocleidomastoid with scapular retractors such as the rhomboids and the trapezius.

prompt: Seated with the knee bent, the client draws the foot up toward the shin against the therapist's hand, and a tendon tightens across the front of the ankle. Which action is tibialis anterior producing?

options.text: Plantarflexion, pointing the foot downward away from the shin
Eversion, turning the sole outward with the fibularis muscles
Knee extension, straightening the leg fully at the tibiofemoral joint
Dorsiflexion, lifting the foot upward toward the anterior shin

explanation: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot. Pulling the foot toward the shin against resistance, with the tendon visible on the anterior ankle, is the dorsiflexion action. Plantarflexion and eversion belong to the calf and fibularis group, and this muscle does not extend the knee.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses dorsiflexion with plantarflexion, the opposite ankle action produced mainly by the calf muscles.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses tibialis anterior with the fibularis muscles, which evert the foot.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an ankle action with knee extension, which is the job of the quadriceps.

prompt: The therapist compares two joints on the same client. The shoulder can flex, extend, abduct, adduct, and rotate, while the elbow mainly bends and straightens. Which type of joint is the shoulder?

options.text: Hinge joint, designed mainly for flexion and extension in a single plane
Pivot joint, designed mainly for rotation around one longitudinal axis
Plane joint, designed mainly for limited gliding between flat surfaces
Ball-and-socket joint, designed for movement through several planes

explanation: The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket, so the humeral head can move in several planes: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation. The elbow is the hinge in this comparison. Pivot and plane joints allow rotation or gliding, not this combination of shoulder motions.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the shoulder with a hinge joint such as the elbow, which mainly flexes and extends.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the shoulder with a pivot joint, which rotates around a single axis, as at the proximal radioulnar joint.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the shoulder with a plane joint, which allows small gliding motions rather than wide angular movement.

prompt: Seated on the edge of a table with the foot hanging free, the client straightens the knee from a bent position and the foot never touches the floor. Which muscle group is the prime mover?

options.text: Hamstrings, which flex the knee and extend the hip behind the thigh
Gastrocnemius, which points the foot down and can also bend the knee
Adductors, which draw the thigh medially toward the opposite leg
Quadriceps femoris, the group that straightens the knee

explanation: The quadriceps femoris group is the prime mover of knee extension. Straightening the knee in sitting, with the foot free, is an open-chain extension driven by that group. Hamstrings and gastrocnemius flex the knee, and the adductors move the thigh toward the midline.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses knee extension with the hamstrings, which flex the knee and extend the hip.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the quadriceps with gastrocnemius, which plantarflexes the ankle and assists knee flexion.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses knee extension with the hip adductors, which draw the thigh toward the midline.

prompt: During intake a first-time client asks what they are agreeing to before any hands-on work begins. Which elements belong in that consent conversation?

options.text: Nature of the work, benefits, risks, alternatives, and a voluntary agreement
Nature of the work plus a waiver that releases the therapist from liability for harm
A single intake signature treated as permission for later visits without another conversation
The therapist's diagnosis of the complaint and a promised cure from the massage

explanation: Informed consent means the client understands what the session involves, the likely benefits and risks, and other options, and agrees freely. That agreement can be changed or withdrawn later, so it is a conversation rather than a one-time release from responsibility.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a liability waiver with informed consent, which requires understanding of benefits, risks, and alternatives.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses one intake signature with ongoing consent, which the client may modify or withdraw at a later visit.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses consent with a medical diagnosis and a promised cure, both of which are outside massage scope.

prompt: A chart note labels the client's condition a relative contraindication, and the client asks whether that cancels today's massage. What does that label allow?

options.text: Postpone the entire session until that condition has completely resolved
Continue after adapting the work or confirming physician clearance
Leave one region untouched and treat the rest of the body at the usual depth
Provide the usual session because a signed consent form removes the need to adapt technique

explanation: A relative contraindication does not automatically cancel care and does not mean the usual session is unchanged. The therapist adapts pressure, positioning, or duration, or seeks physician clearance, based on how the condition presents that day.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a relative contraindication with an absolute one that postpones treatment of the whole body.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a relative contraindication with a local one, which avoids a region and treats elsewhere as usual.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a signed consent form with clinical permission to skip modification or physician clearance.

prompt: After the session the therapist writes that guarded lumbar motion fits the client's reported lifting strain. Which SOAP section should hold that clinical impression?

options.text: Activities, meaning the client's daily tasks and the goals stated at intake
Allergies, meaning sensitivities and reactions the client reported in the health history
Assessment, the therapist's clinical impression of how the findings fit
Advice, meaning the home-care steps given to the client at the end of the visit

explanation: SOAP separates the client's story, measurable findings, the therapist's impression, and the plan. Linking guarded lumbar motion with a reported lifting strain is an assessment, not a list of goals, allergies, or home care.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses assessment with subjective content, where daily tasks and the client's stated goals are recorded.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses assessment with health-history details such as allergies, which are subjective information.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses assessment with the plan, where home-care advice given at the end of the visit is written.

prompt: While planning neck and shoulder work, the therapist flags the axilla and the upper abdomen for a lighter approach. Why do those areas call for that change?

options.text: Compressed points there send pain to distant regions that the chart should map in detail
Those muscles are the most hypertonic and therefore need the deepest sustained pressure
Bony landmarks there are palpated to confirm where each muscle attaches to the skeleton
Underlying structures call for caution or avoidance of deep pressure

explanation: Endangerment sites are places where nerves, vessels, or organs lie near the surface. The axilla and upper abdomen are classic examples, so deep pressure is lightened or avoided rather than used because the muscles feel tight.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses endangerment sites with trigger points, which refer pain to distant regions when compressed.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the pressure rule: these sites need a lighter plan because vessels, nerves, or organs lie close.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses endangerment sites with bony landmarks used to locate where muscles attach.

prompt: At the opening of a back massage the therapist wants to spread oil and warm the tissue before any specific work. Which stroke fits that opening purpose?

options.text: Gliding strokes that spread lubricant and warm the tissue
Kneading strokes that lift, squeeze, and release the muscle belly
Percussive strokes such as hacking, cupping, and rhythmic tapping on the back
Small circular strokes worked across the direction of the muscle fibers

explanation: Swedish strokes are grouped by what they do. Effleurage is the long gliding stroke used to apply lubricant, introduce touch, and warm tissue before narrower work such as kneading, friction, or percussion.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses effleurage with petrissage, the kneading stroke that lifts and squeezes the muscle belly.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses effleurage with tapotement, the percussive strokes that include hacking, cupping, and tapping.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses effleurage with friction, the small cross-fiber stroke used on a specific spot.

prompt: Six weeks after a lateral ankle sprain, a client has a stable cord-like adhesion along the ligament and asks for work on that band once screening is clear. Which technique matches?

options.text: Light rhythmic strokes swept toward the nearest lymph nodes to move fluid out of the foot
Cautious cross-fiber friction to mobilize the adhesion
Slow broad gliding strokes intended to quiet the nervous system across the whole limb
Sustained compression held on a tender point until the referral pattern eases

explanation: Deep transverse friction is a specific cross-fiber stroke used to mobilize scar and adhesions in a tendon or ligament. It can be uncomfortable, so it waits until screening shows the acute hot swollen phase has passed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses transverse friction with manual lymphatic drainage, which uses light rhythmic strokes toward nodes.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses transverse friction with slow effleurage, which glides broadly to relax rather than work a scar band.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses transverse friction with trigger-point compression, which holds pressure instead of moving across fibers.

prompt: A client reports losing weight without trying and pain that wakes them at night and does not ease when they change position. They ask for massage of that area as a simple muscle strain. What should the therapist do?

options.text: Proceed with light Swedish massage and suggest a doctor visit if pain persists
Treat the painful area with deep tissue to reduce night pain and then reassess
Refer to a physician; do not treat as simple musculoskeletal without clearance
Document the symptoms and continue treatment until the next scheduled session

explanation: Unexplained weight loss plus night pain that wakes the client and does not change with position is a red-flag pattern for possible serious disease, such as infection or malignancy, rather than an ordinary muscle strain. The therapist does not diagnose the cause. The client is referred to a physician, and the area is not worked as simple musculoskeletal pain until it has been medically cleared.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a red-flag pattern with a wait-and-see plan; referral comes before treating the pain as a muscle strain.
distractorExplanations.b: Deep work over unexplained night pain can mask or worsen serious pathology; medical clearance comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Documenting red flags is required, but continuing treatment without referral delays needed medical evaluation.

prompt: A client arrives with a hot, swollen calf that started yesterday, plus calf pain when the foot is dorsiflexed. What should the therapist do?

options.text: Use light gliding toward the heart to ease the swelling in the calf
Massage the foot below the swelling and prop the limb up on a bolster
Apply moist heat and gentle stretching to ease the discomfort in the calf
Do not massage and refer the client for urgent medical care

explanation: A calf that became hot and swollen overnight is treated as a possible deep-vein thrombosis until a clinician clears it. Pain when the foot is dorsiflexed is not a reliable test and does not make the calf safe to touch. Massage on that limb is withheld, including light or distal work, and the client is referred for urgent care. The therapist does not diagnose the clot.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a possible deep-vein thrombosis with ordinary swelling that light centripetal gliding might ease.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a possible clot with a local sore spot, where work away from the area might be considered.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a possible clot with a muscle cramp that heat and stretching would be used to ease.

prompt: Before table work the therapist compares ears, shoulders, pelvis, and ankles with a plumb line from the front, side, and back. What is that screen mainly gathering?

options.text: How landmarks line up from several views, including side-to-side differences
How far each major joint moves when the client performs active and passive range testing
How much force each muscle group can hold while the therapist applies manual resistance
How the client walks, including stride length, arm swing, and weight shift across the room

explanation: Static posture assessment compares landmarks such as the ears, shoulders, pelvis, and ankles with a plumb line from more than one view. Those asymmetries guide the session and are separate from joint-motion tests, strength grades, and walking observation.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a standing landmark screen with range-of-motion testing, which measures how far joints move.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses postural assessment with manual muscle testing, which grades strength against resistance.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a standing posture screen with gait analysis, which watches stride and weight shift while walking.

prompt: Two days after a fall, a client's knee is warm, swollen, and unstable, and a hamstring stretch reproduces sharp pain. What is the appropriate choice about stretching?

options.text: Use a firm hamstring stretch, treating the knee as ordinary chronic tightness from sitting all week
Skip the hamstring stretch while the knee is inflamed, unstable, and sharply painful
Lengthen the stretch because gliding strokes have already warmed the thigh tissue thoroughly
Push the stretch to restore motion that a few inactive days have temporarily reduced

explanation: A knee that is warm, swollen, and unstable two days after a fall, with sharp pain during a hamstring stretch, is protected rather than stretched. Inflammation, instability, and that pain response are contraindications to the stretch, so a shorter or firmer version is not a safe adaptation. Stretching fits chronic tightness only after the tissue is ready.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an acute injured knee with chronic tightness, which can be a reason to stretch once tissue is ready.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses warming tissue, a normal preparation, with permission to stretch an inflamed unstable joint.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses stiffness from a few inactive days with an acute injury that needs protection from a firm stretch.

prompt: While updating the intake, the therapist sorts harmless preferences from findings that can make massage unsafe today. Which group belongs in the stop-and-reconsider set?

options.text: Seasonal allergies the client describes as well controlled on a daily medication
A suspected clot, a contagious rash, or a fever that is not controlled
A request for lavender oil because the client prefers that scent in the treatment room
A childhood scar the client says has been fully healed for many years and causes no trouble

explanation: Acute deep-vein thrombosis, a contagious skin infection, and a fever that is not controlled are serious contraindications. They are screened before massage because treatment could move a clot, spread infection, or overlook a systemic illness.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a stable seasonal allergy with a finding that would halt or sharply limit massage today.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a scent preference with a health finding that changes whether massage is safe to begin.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a long-healed scar with an active local or systemic reason to stop and reconsider the session.

prompt: A colleague demonstrates long superficial passes from the iliac crest toward the shoulders, then asks which Swedish category that pass belongs to.

options.text: Rhythmic percussion such as hacking and tapping across the back muscles
Gliding passes that warm tissue and spread lubricant
Kneading that lifts, squeezes, and then releases the muscle belly
Fine trembling or shaking kept on one small area of skin for a minute

explanation: A long superficial pass that slides along the skin is effleurage, the gliding Swedish stroke used to warm tissue and distribute lubricant. Petrissage kneads, tapotement strikes, and vibration shakes, so those categories do not describe this pass.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a gliding pass with tapotement, the percussive category that includes hacking and tapping.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a gliding pass with petrissage, which lifts and squeezes rather than sliding along the skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a gliding pass with vibration, the fine trembling stroke kept on one small area.

prompt: A student sinks firm pressure into the femoral triangle on the anterior thigh and asks why the chart marks that hollow as an endangerment site.

options.text: Tender points there send pain into distant regions when they are pressed for a long hold
The femoral nerve and vessels in that hollow are poorly protected from pressure
Muscle attachments there are confirmed by pressing along the bony rim of the pelvis
Lymph nodes there are expected to receive deep sustained pressure during the thigh routine

explanation: The femoral triangle is an endangerment site because the femoral nerve and the femoral vessels lie there with little protection. Firm pressure in that hollow is avoided so those structures are not compressed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an endangerment site with a trigger point, which refers pain when a tender spot is compressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an endangerment site with a bony landmark used to locate muscle attachments on the pelvis.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the caution: nodes and vessels at an endangerment site need light contact, not deep sustained pressure.

prompt: The therapist records shoulder heights, measured neck rotation, and a ropey band found on palpation. Which SOAP section should hold those entries?

options.text: Subjective notes: reported pain, history, and the goals the client named at the start of the visit
Objective notes: posture, measured motion, and palpation findings
Assessment notes: the therapist's view of progress and how the tissues responded today
Plan notes: home-care advice and the date chosen for the client's next appointment

explanation: The objective section stores what the therapist can see or measure, including posture, range of motion, and palpation. The client's story stays subjective, the interpretation stays in assessment, and later advice stays in the plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses objective findings with subjective content such as pain ratings, history, and stated goals.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses measured findings with assessment, where the therapist interprets progress and tissue response.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses clinical observations with the plan, where home care and the next appointment are written.

prompt: If a client reports sharp neurological pain radiating with cervical compression signs, the safest action is often to:

options.text: Continue with deep cervical work to release the compressed nerve root
Stop or modify treatment and refer for appropriate medical evaluation
Apply traction and strong stretching to decompress the cervical spine
Finish the session as planned and recommend rest if symptoms continue

explanation: Radiating pain with cervical compression signs suggests nerve-root irritation. Deep pressure, traction, and strong stretching can worsen that irritation. The therapist does not diagnose the nerve problem. The session is stopped or modified, and the client is referred for medical evaluation.

distractorExplanations.a: Deep cervical pressure can aggravate nerve root compression; radiating neurologic signs call for referral.
distractorExplanations.c: Forceful traction and stretching of a compromised cervical spine are risky and beyond the massage scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Finishing as planned ignores neurologic red flags and delays the medical evaluation the client needs.

prompt: At 28 weeks of pregnancy a client is unable to lie face-down comfortably and feels short of breath when lying flat on the back. How should the session be positioned?

options.text: Supported side-lying, without long prone or flat supine positioning
Prone on a standard table so the usual back routine can stay unchanged for the full hour
Flat on the back with a heavy knee bolster for the entire hour despite the breathlessness
