A chair massage alone, because pregnancy means table work is no longer an appropriate choice

explanation: Later in an uncomplicated pregnancy, supported side-lying avoids prone pressure on the abdomen and avoids flat supine pressure of the uterus on the vena cava, which can cause shortness of breath. Pregnancy by itself does not cancel the session.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a standard prone back routine with positioning that fits a 28-week pregnancy and reported breathlessness.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a knee bolster with a fix for flat supine lying, which can compress the vena cava and worsen breathlessness.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a positioning change with a ban on table massage for an uncomplicated pregnancy.

prompt: Yesterday a client sprained an ankle. Today that lateral ankle is hot, puffy, and too tender for pressure, while the rest of the body feels fine. How should the region be handled?

options.text: Skip the acute ankle and treat regions that tolerate touch
Apply deep cross-fiber friction directly on the swollen lateral ankle joint
Use vigorous percussion over the swelling to drive fluid out of the joint capsule
Stretch the ankle hard so full motion returns before the client leaves today

explanation: A hot, puffy, newly sprained ankle is a local contraindication. The injured region is left alone while other areas may be massaged if the client is otherwise well. Deep friction, percussion, and a hard stretch can increase inflammation.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a local contraindication with a scar-adhesion technique, which is not used on a hot swollen ankle from yesterday.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses acute swelling with a cue for percussion, which can irritate inflamed tissue over a new sprain.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an acute sprain with stiffness that a hard stretch would be used to chase before the visit ends.

prompt: An older client with known osteoporosis asks for the same deep pressure used last year on the back and ribs. What adjustment belongs in today's plan?

options.text: Use broader, lighter pressure and avoid hard twisting over fragile bone
Increase pressure, because older back muscles need stronger input before they will relax today
Add high-velocity thrusts through the thoracic spine in order to free each rib
Percuss firmly along the rib cage so local circulation is strongly stimulated

explanation: Osteoporosis is a special-population caution because heavy pressure, percussion, and aggressive twisting raise the risk of fracture. The session can continue with broader, lighter strokes matched to bone health rather than last year's deep-pressure request.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses fragile bone with a reason to press harder, which raises fracture risk over the ribs and spine.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a massage plan with high-velocity thrusting, which is outside scope and risky over osteoporotic bone.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a circulation goal with firm percussion, a stroke that can injure fragile ribs.

prompt: A client arrives flushed and shivering, reporting a temperature taken this morning well above their usual reading, plus body aches. What is the appropriate session decision?

options.text: Postpone the session and refer the client for medical care of this fever
Shorten the hour and use very deep pressure in an attempt to drive the fever down
Massage the back, because a fever is described as unrelated to the muscles being treated
Continue the visit if the client signs a form that accepts the fever risk today

explanation: Fever with chills and body aches is a systemic contraindication, so the session is postponed and the client is referred for medical care. The therapist does not treat the illness. Soft-tissue work can further stress the body, and a shorter or deeper massage is not a substitute for that referral.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses fever with a muscle problem that deep pressure could treat, and delays care for a systemic illness.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a systemic contraindication with a local one by treating the back while fever and aches are present.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a signed risk form with clearance to massage during an uncontrolled febrile illness.

prompt: Long-standing visible varicose veins cross the medial lower leg, without sudden puffiness or warmth, and the client asks for deep stripping along those veins. What plan fits?

options.text: Deliver deep stripping along each vein toward the hip in order to empty the vessel
Use heavy percussion directly on the vein so the vessel wall tone is expected to improve
Skip deep strokes on the veins and use lighter contact nearby
Warm the vein with a pack first, then strip the leg using the deepest strokes available today

explanation: Varicose veins are a local contraindication to deep pressure directly on the vessel, because the wall is already distended. Nearby tissue can receive lighter contact when the area is not hot, suddenly swollen, or otherwise suggestive of a clot.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a distended vein with a muscle that deep stripping toward the hip would be used to flush.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a fragile surface vein with a target for heavy percussion aimed at changing vessel tone.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a local vessel caution with a heat-then-deep-stroke sequence that loads the vein further.

prompt: Watching the client walk in, the therapist sees a short stance phase on the right and the trunk leaning left. How should that observation shape the session?

options.text: Ignore the walk, because gait has no bearing on how a table session is planned or recorded
Name a torn meniscus in the note and recommend that the client schedule surgery
Record the gait and let it guide which regions are assessed
Cancel care until a physician has fully corrected the walking pattern before any visit

explanation: Gait is part of client assessment. A short right stance and a trunk lean are objective findings that are written down and used to decide where to look next. They are not a medical diagnosis and they do not by themselves cancel care.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses gait with an optional extra, ignoring walking findings that belong in the assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses observation of a short stance with a diagnosis of a torn meniscus and a surgical recommendation.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a gait finding with an absolute reason to cancel, before the rest of the assessment is done.

prompt: While contacting the upper trapezius the therapist feels a warm, boggy spot that is more tender than the surrounding muscle. What should those palpation findings do?

options.text: Stay out of the note, because the chart is meant to hold the client's spoken story and nothing felt
Count as proof of a fracture, so the visit ends immediately without any further questions
Be noted as tissue quality and compared with the intake complaint
Require deep friction on that spot until the warmth can no longer be felt by the therapist

explanation: Palpation collects objective information about temperature, texture, and tenderness. A warm, boggy, tender spot is recorded and matched against the complaint. It does not by itself prove a fracture, and it is not a cue to friction the area until the sign disappears.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses palpation with optional color, leaving temperature, texture, and tenderness out of the objective note.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a warm boggy spot in the trapezius with proof of a fracture that ends the visit at once.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a palpation finding with a goal to erase warmth through deep friction before the session moves on.

prompt: Intake shows the goal is turning the head to check traffic, and neck rotation is limited toward the right. What is the best use of that information?

options.text: Set the driving goal aside and give this client the same full-body routine used for every other visitor
Promise that one visit will restore a normal turning range for checking traffic lanes
Build the session around that goal and recheck rotation afterward
Work the low back instead, treating neck motion as something massage does not address

explanation: Treatment planning ties the session to the stated goal and the assessment finding. Here that means addressing the neck limitation that affects driving and checking rotation again afterward, without promising that one visit will restore normal motion.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an individual goal with a fixed full-body routine that ignores the driving complaint and the motion limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a treatment goal with a promise that one session will restore normal neck rotation for driving.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a neck-motion goal with work on the low back, as if neck rotation were outside massage care.

prompt: A bumped forearm is puffy and warm this morning, skin sensation is intact, and the client asks about a cold pack. When is cold a reasonable local choice?

options.text: Cold is saved for chronic stiffness that has already lasted many months without any recent bump
Cold is a poor match for new puffiness and should be replaced with a hot pack on the forearm
Cold can ease a new local injury when skin sensation is intact
Cold belongs on skin that feels numb, and it can stay in place for the whole visit

explanation: Cold is often chosen soon after a local injury to ease pain and help limit puffiness, provided skin sensation is intact so the client can feel when the pack is too intense. A hot pack is a poorer match for a forearm that was bumped this morning, and numb skin is a reason to avoid cold.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an acute bump with chronic stiffness, which is a more typical time to consider heat rather than cold.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the early injury window with a reason to choose heat, which can increase circulation in warm puffy tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses intact sensation, a safety requirement for cold, with numb skin that cannot report an overly intense pack.

prompt: A prescribed blood thinner makes this client bruise after ordinary bumps, and the client asks for the deepest pressure available. How should today's plan change?

options.text: Use heavier pressure so the medication is less able to limit the effect the client wants from the session
Cancel the visit, because taking a prescription means hands-on work is prohibited in every case
Lighten pressure and watch the skin, because bruising risk is higher
Add cupping and heavy percussion to move blood along despite the prescribed medication

explanation: Anticoagulant therapy is a special-population caution. Clotting is reduced, so pressure stays lighter and the therapist watches the skin for bruising. The medication is not a reason to press harder, and it is not an automatic ban on every massage.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a bleeding risk with a reason to use heavier pressure so the medication will not blunt the session.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a prescription caution with a total ban, skipping the lighter session that can still be appropriate.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses anticoagulant caution with cupping and heavy percussion, which raise the chance of bruising.

prompt: After several minutes of lifting and squeezing the calf muscle, the client asks what effect that stroke is having. Which description fits?

options.text: Effleurage, a long glide used mainly to spread oil and settle the client before specific work on the calf
Vibration, a fine shake that stays on the skin and does not lift the muscle belly at all
Tapotement, rhythmic striking used to stimulate the calf rather than lift and squeeze it
Petrissage, lifting muscle to mobilize it and increase local flow

explanation: Petrissage kneads by lifting and squeezing muscle. That mobilizes the tissue and is taught as increasing local circulation, which matches the calf work just described. Gliding, shaking, and striking are different Swedish categories with different effects.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses kneading with effleurage, the gliding stroke used to spread oil and introduce touch.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses kneading with vibration, a fine shake that does not lift and squeeze the muscle belly.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses kneading with tapotement, the striking stroke used for stimulation rather than lifting muscle.

prompt: A returning client mentions a new prescription and a surgery scheduled for next week, then starts to lie down immediately. Where do those facts belong before hands-on work?

options.text: In the plan section that is written after the hands-on work is already finished for the day
In the billing notes, so they can be skipped when the health update is reviewed
In place of posture and movement observation, which the new facts make unnecessary today
In an updated intake so the plan can be adapted before touch

explanation: Session organization starts with a current intake. A new medication and upcoming surgery can change pressure, positioning, and whether to treat, so they are collected before massage. They do not replace posture observation or wait for the closing note.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses pre-session screening with the plan written afterward, when pressure and positioning can no longer be adapted.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses health information that changes the session with billing details that can be left out of the update.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an intake update with a substitute for posture and movement observation, which still inform the plan.

prompt: The client wants a hot pack on a knee that turned red and puffy after a twist last night. What is the safer decision about heat?

options.text: Use the hottest pack on hand so the new puffiness is forced to leave the knee before the session
Apply heat, because warmth is considered useful from the first night of healing onward
Switch the pack from hot to cold every minute until the redness has faded from the knee
Skip the hot pack while the knee is acutely inflamed

explanation: Heat increases local circulation and is a poor match for a knee that became red and puffy after a twist last night. Acute inflammation is a contraindication to the hot pack; the area is protected rather than warmed further.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses acute puffiness with a problem that the hottest pack would drive out of the knee.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses heat's usefulness in later stiffness with permission to heat a knee on the first night of inflammation.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a contraindication to heat with a rapid hot-cold cycle aimed at making redness fade during the visit.

prompt: Diabetic neuropathy has removed light-touch sensation from both feet, and the client asks for a hot stone on each sole. What precaution comes first?

options.text: Place the hottest stones on the soles, since the client will not feel it if a stone is too intense
Skip further questions, because lost sensation is taken to mean massage will be more effective
Use deep specific friction on both soles in an effort to wake the nerves before the stones
Skip heat on the numb feet and keep pressure light with skin checks

explanation: Reduced sensation from diabetic neuropathy is a special-population risk. The client cannot reliably report that a stone is too hot or that pressure is too hard, so heat is avoided on the numb feet and any contact stays light with visual skin checks.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses lost sensation with permission to use the hottest stones, removing the client's ability to report a burn.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses neuropathy with a benefit, skipping the questions and precautions that insensate skin requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses numb soles with a target for deep friction meant to wake nerves, which can injure tissue the client cannot feel.

prompt: Ten minutes into a firm back routine the client tenses, holds their breath, and says the pressure is too much. What should the therapist do next?

options.text: Hold the same pressure so the back tissue can adapt before the scheduled hour runs out
End the professional relationship, because any discomfort means massage is contraindicated for this person
Move to the neck and use the deeper pressure that was written in the original session plan
Lighten up, recheck comfort, and change the rest of the plan

explanation: Treatment planning stays responsive during the session. Guarding, breath-holding, and a direct request are feedback to lighten the work and revise the plan. Pushing through, shifting the same depth to the neck, or ending the relationship misreads that feedback.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses guarding and a direct request with a reason to keep the same pressure until the tissue adapts.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses in-session discomfort with a contraindication that ends the professional relationship.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a pressure complaint with a cue to relocate the deeper work to the neck as originally planned.

prompt: A spouse telephones the front desk and asks what the practitioner found in yesterday's shoulder session.

options.text: Withhold the findings and release them with the client's consent or a legal duty to disclose
Summarize the shoulder findings for the caller, because a spouse is presumed to share decisions about care, recovery, and home instructions
Describe yesterday's session to the friend who referred this person and arranged the original booking
Give a full report now that the series has ended and the file is being treated as inactive

explanation: Health information from a session stays confidential. Marriage, a referral, and the end of care do not authorize disclosure. Share findings with the client's consent or when a specific legal duty, such as a mandated report, applies.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a marital tie with authorization; a spouse still needs permission before session findings are shared.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a referral or booking role with membership on the care team; the referrer has no right to health details.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses discharge with the end of privacy; the duty of confidentiality continues after the relationship ends.

prompt: A long-standing client invites the massage therapist to manage rental housing on weekends while weekly appointments continue.

options.text: Treat every social or business contact outside the treatment room as an automatic ethics violation, including a wave in a grocery aisle
Decline the housing role if it would cloud clinical judgment or expose the client to exploitation
Accept the housing role because a business deal between adults is separate from care and needs no ethics review
Accept the housing role once a signed form states that the outside job is welcome

explanation: A second relationship is unethical when it impairs professional judgment or risks exploiting the client. A wave in public is not that kind of relationship. A business deal is not exempt from ethics review, and a permission form does not repair a tie that can skew care.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses any outside contact with an unethical dual relationship; incidental contact is not itself a violation.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a separate business deal with an ethics exemption; managing this client's housing can still bias judgment and exploit the relationship.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a signed permission form with sound judgment; consent does not cure exploitation or clouded decisions.

prompt: During the session a client comments sexually on the therapist's hands and expects the work to continue unchanged.

options.text: Treat intercourse as the sole form of misconduct and file the comment under personal taste rather than professional ethics
Bar sexual contact during the hour but agree to a date once this appointment is over
Stop the sexualized comment and keep sexual behavior out of the relationship with this client
Keep working and treat the comment as harmless flirting so the client does not feel criticized

explanation: Sexual misconduct includes sexual comments, jokes, gestures, and contact with a client, not intercourse alone. A date after this appointment still sexualizes a current professional relationship. Minimizing the comment as flirting and continuing the work leaves the boundary unaddressed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses intercourse with the whole category; sexual comments and gestures toward a client are misconduct as well.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the end of one appointment with permission to sexualize the relationship with a person still in care.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses keeping the client comfortable with a sound boundary; a sexual comment is stopped, not passed off as harmless flirting.

prompt: A client asks for a spinal adjustment the therapist practiced last month in a weekend continuing-education class.

options.text: Perform the adjustment because a course certificate authorizes every method the weekend class demonstrated to participants
Perform the adjustment because it was permitted where the therapist originally attended school
Perform the adjustment because the client requested it and signed consent before lying down
Decline the adjustment unless training and the law that governs this practice both allow it

explanation: Scope of practice is set by the therapist's education and by the law where the service is given. A continuing-education class does not widen that legal scope. Client consent cannot authorize a technique the practice act places outside massage.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a continuing-education certificate with legal scope; a class does not expand the practice act.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the place of training with the place of practice; scope follows the law where the work is performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses consent with scope; a client's request cannot authorize a service outside education and law.

prompt: Halfway through the hour the client says the neck work feels wrong and asks that the neck be left alone.

options.text: Stop the neck work at once and honor the refusal without pressure to continue
Continue the planned neck sequence because the therapist believes the work serves the client's own good and long-term comfort
Finish the planned neck work because consent given at the start cannot be withdrawn
Note the request and then finish the neck sequence so the chart shows the concern was heard

explanation: Informed refusal is part of autonomy. The client may decline a region during the session, and the therapist stops that work without pressure. Consent given at the start can be withdrawn. A chart note of the request does not authorize finishing the neck sequence.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the therapist's belief about benefit with authority to override a refusal; forcing a region is unethical.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses intake consent with a permanent lock; agreement can be withdrawn at any point in the session.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a chart note with consent to continue; writing down the request does not authorize finishing the neck sequence.

prompt: The bookkeeper asks why each paid visit needs a matching receipt instead of a year-end total from memory.

options.text: Receipts exist so an insurer will accept client satisfaction as proof that the visit produced a clinical result
Receipts support tax reporting, legal compliance, and a transparent business relationship with the client
Receipts replace the clinical note as the legal record of the techniques used that day
Keep a year-end total from memory because a per-visit receipt is a courtesy the client must request

explanation: Honest billing records support taxes, legal compliance, and a clear business relationship. They document payment, not clinical results, and they do not replace the treatment note. A total reconstructed from memory is not a substitute for a receipt made when the client pays.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a payment record with outcome evidence; a receipt shows that a payment was collected, not that the session produced a clinical result.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a receipt with the treatment record; clinical documentation is a separate account of the session.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a courtesy copy with the clinic's record; a receipt is written when the client pays, even if the client never asks for a copy.

prompt: A new graduate wants the website headline to read physician-level pain specialist after taking a pathology course.

options.text: Add a medical-doctor title because pathology class covered disease, even without a medical degree
Promise visitors that massage cures cancer so the headline gives callers a certain medical outcome to expect
Use titles actually earned and avoid language that implies a medical license
Place a coworker's license number on the page so the site shows an active credential

explanation: Advertising must use credentials the therapist legally earned. Implying a medical license, inventing a degree, guaranteeing a cure, or using someone else's license misleads the public and can be unlawful.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a pathology course with a medical degree; claiming to be a physician without that degree is fraud.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses bold marketing with an allowed claim; guaranteeing that massage cures cancer is deceptive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a coworker's license with one's own; using another person's license number is misrepresentation.

prompt: The client lies prone, in pain, and partly undressed, then agrees to every suggestion without asking a question.

options.text: Treat the client as the more powerful person because payment and the session goals come from the person on the table
Treat both people as equals the moment the consent form is signed at the start of care
Treat the imbalance as finished after the client has returned for several weekly visits
Recognize the therapist's greater influence and refuse to use it for personal advantage

explanation: The therapeutic relationship carries a power differential. Knowledge, the setting, pain, and partial undress leave the client vulnerable, even when the client pays and signs consent. The therapist must not exploit that influence, and the imbalance lasts across the relationship.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses payment with power; paying the fee does not outweigh the client's vulnerability in the session.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a signed consent form with equal power; consent does not remove the therapist's greater influence.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses familiarity with equality; the power differential continues across later visits, not the first ones alone.

prompt: After the session the therapist urges an unneeded, high-priced supplement because each bottle pays a personal commission.

options.text: Recognize a conflict of interest when personal profit drives advice the client did not need
Treat the pitch as the same duty as sending red-flag symptoms to a physician for a prompt medical evaluation
Treat the pitch as the same practice as posting one consistent fee for every person who books
Treat the pitch as the same help as teaching a home stretch the client can practice at no charge

explanation: A conflict of interest arises when the therapist's financial gain steers the client toward something unnecessary. Referring red-flag findings, charging a consistent published fee, and teaching a free home stretch serve the client and are not a commission-driven product pitch.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a physician referral for red flags with self-dealing; that referral serves the client rather than a commission.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a consistent published fee with a conflict; transparent pricing does not steer an unneeded purchase.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses free self-care instruction with a sales pitch; a home stretch brings the therapist no personal profit.

prompt: During the health history the client mentions several private facts, and the therapist must judge which one can require a statutory report.

options.text: Past drug use mentioned in a single sentence, with no statement of current harm to the client or to anyone else
Suspected abuse of a child or an older adult where the law designates this profession to report
HIV status volunteered while the intake form was being completed in the treatment room
A coworker's pattern of arriving late to appointments already printed on the schedule

explanation: Where the law makes a massage therapist a mandated reporter, suspected abuse of a child or an older adult can override ordinary confidentiality. Past substance use without current danger, HIV status, and a coworker's lateness are not that kind of report.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses confidential health history with a mandated report; past drug use without current risk stays private.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a sensitive diagnosis with a reporting duty; HIV status shared at intake remains confidential.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses workplace punctuality with a statutory duty; a coworker's lateness is an employment matter.

prompt: A first-time client is seated, and the therapist is deciding what must occur before any hands-on work begins.

options.text: Obtain a liability waiver that becomes irrevocable as soon as the first stroke is delivered and the session clock starts
Explain the plan, the relevant risks and benefits, and secure agreement before any touch
Save the explanation of the plan until afterward so the client does not feel anxious
Take a verbal yes from the friend who booked the hour on the client's behalf

explanation: Informed consent means the client understands the plan, including risks and benefits that matter for this session, and agrees before treatment. Consent can be withdrawn; it is not an irrevocable waiver. The person who booked the visit cannot consent in the client's place.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a liability waiver with informed consent; agreement can be withdrawn and is not locked by the first stroke.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses reassurance with consent; explaining the plan after the work means the client agreed to nothing beforehand.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the person who scheduled the visit with the client; consent comes from the client or a legal guardian.

prompt: The practitioner starts a romantic relationship with someone currently receiving bodywork and also collects that person's rent.

options.text: Welcome the overlap because it raises trust and makes the person follow the home-care plan more closely between visits
Treat the overlap as a problem because it can create a conflict of interest and a boundary breach
Treat the overlap as a crime everywhere simply because a second role exists
Treat the overlap as a problem mainly because it reduces income from repeat visits

explanation: When a romantic or financial relationship overlaps current care, judgment can shift toward protecting that other role. That is a conflict of interest and a boundary problem. The harm is to client welfare, not to the therapist's income, and a second role is not automatically a crime in every setting.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses blurred roles with healthy trust; the overlap compromises objectivity instead of strengthening appropriate trust.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an ethics concern with a universal crime; the problem here is the conflict of interest and the boundary breach.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses revenue with the ethical harm; the risk is biased judgment and a boundary breach, not a smaller income.

prompt: Colleagues who do not treat this person request the name and diagnosis, and a marketer wants blurred posture photos online.

options.text: Tell inquiring relatives how the plan is progressing whenever they telephone the clinic for an update on recovery
Protect the health information and disclose it with authorization or a legal requirement
Identify the person and the diagnosis to colleagues who have no role in the care
Publish the blurred photos without asking, because the face is hidden from view

explanation: Confidentiality limits disclosure to what the client authorizes or what the law requires. Relatives, uninvolved coworkers, and marketers do not gain a need to know by asking. Blurring a face does not replace permission to use images.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a family phone call with authorization; relatives need the client's permission before progress is discussed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses curiosity with a treatment role; coworkers outside the care have no need to hear the name or diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a hidden face with consent; blurred photos still require the client's permission before publication.

prompt: Pointing to a new lump, the client lists possible next steps and asks which one a massage therapist should refuse because it falls outside scope.

options.text: Observe standing posture and the range of joint motion before the session plan is chosen for today
Assign a disease name to the lump and recommend a prescription medicine to treat it
Demonstrate a self-care stretch that stays inside the therapist's training
Record the health history and refer the lump to a physician for evaluation

explanation: Diagnosing disease and prescribing medication sit outside massage scope in United States practice acts. Postural and motion assessment, self-care stretches within training, a health history, and referral of red flags are part of professional massage practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an in-scope posture and motion check with diagnosis; observing movement is allowed, naming a disease is excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a prescription with home care; a stretch inside the therapist's training is generally within massage scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses referral with diagnosis; a health history and a physician referral for a red flag stay inside massage duties.

prompt: A client offers a large personal favor and says the therapist, as the expert, should decide matters in the client's home life.

options.text: Accept the favor because paying for sessions gives the client greater authority than the therapist who provides the work
Decline the favor and remember that professional authority must not be used to exploit the client
Accept the favor because friendship between the two people removes the imbalance
Accept the favor because a signed consent form makes the two people equal decision makers

explanation: The therapist holds professional authority, and the client is vulnerable, especially when unclothed or in pain. Payment, friendship, and a consent signature do not erase that power differential. Using authority to steer a client's home life or to accept an exploiting favor is unethical.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses payment with authority; the fee does not give the client more power than the therapist's professional role.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses friendship with equality; a personal relationship is a dual role and does not remove the power differential.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses informed consent with equal power; the signature does not cancel the therapist's professional authority.

prompt: While the client turns from prone to supine, the sheet slips off the chest just as abdominal work is about to start.

options.text: Pause and recover the chest, then uncover the abdomen after the client agrees to that area
Leave the sheet where it fell so the client can see that the therapist feels at ease with exposure and will not interrupt the flow
Ask the client to hold the sheet aside and keep the torso uncovered for the rest of the hour
Wait for the client to object before covering the chest, and otherwise keep working with the chest exposed

explanation: Draping protects privacy and the professional boundary. When the sheet slips, the therapist covers the chest again and exposes only the abdomen, with the client's agreement. The therapist's ease with exposure, a request to hold the sheet aside, or waiting for an objection does not replace that standard.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the therapist's comfort with the client's privacy; an exposed chest still needs to be covered again.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses help holding the sheet with permission to leave the torso bare; the untreated chest stays covered.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a client objection with the draping standard; chest coverage is restored when the sheet slips, without waiting for the client to complain.

prompt: Oil coats the face cradle and the sheets after the last person leaves, and the next person is already waiting.

options.text: Change the linens and clean the cradle and table surface before the next person enters
Flip the sheets over and reuse them so the schedule stays intact for the person who is already waiting in the reception area
Spray a strong fragrance across the table and keep those sheets for the rest of the shift
Ask the waiting person to supply a towel and skip cleaning the cradle this turn

explanation: Each client receives clean linens and a cleaned table and face cradle. Turning sheets over, masking oil with fragrance, or shifting the cleaning duty to the next client leaves residue and undermines sanitation between sessions.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a flipped sheet with a clean one; used linens are replaced, not turned, between clients.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses fragrance with sanitation; scent does not remove oil or ready the surface for the next person.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the client's towel with clinic sanitation; the table and cradle are cleaned by the practice between visits.

prompt: Low-back strain builds after the therapist bends at the waist across a low table to reach a far shoulder.

options.text: Raise the table and shift force through a staggered stance and the legs rather than the waist
Lower the table further so the therapist can perch on the side and stretch even farther across the client's torso to the far shoulder
Keep the same bend because the client's preferred pressure matters more than joint alignment
Lock both knees and twist the spine so one hand can stay on the far shoulder

explanation: Sound body mechanics use table height, a staggered stance, and the legs so the therapist does not hinge at the waist or twist under load. Dropping the table, locking the knees, or sacrificing alignment for pressure raises injury risk without improving the work.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a lower table with better reach; dropping the height increases the waist bend instead of removing it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses client preference with safe mechanics; pressure can be delivered without sacrificing alignment.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a locked, twisted posture with stability; stacked joints and a mobile stance protect the back.

prompt: The session is over and the therapist plans to reconstruct the chart tomorrow, using the phrase seemed fine.

options.text: Enter the note the same day in observable language and store it where authorized staff can read it
Skip the chart because the receipt already lists the time and proves which methods were used
Enter 'seemed fine' tomorrow because that short phrase is an adequate record of the session
Wait until a complaint arrives next week and fill in whatever can still be remembered from the visit

explanation: Treatment records should be completed in a timely way, written in factual language, and kept so that uninvolved people cannot read them. A receipt does not describe the session. 'Seemed fine' is a judgment, not a record of what was done or reported, and waiting for a complaint invites missing detail.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a receipt with clinical documentation; payment proof does not record findings or the work performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a vague impression with documentation; 'seemed fine' does not record the work, the findings, or what the client reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses later memory with a timely record; the note is written from the session, not reconstructed after a complaint.

prompt: A current client asks for the therapist's personal phone number and proposes dinner this weekend apart from appointments.

options.text: Share the personal number and accept dinner if the conversation stays away from clinical topics and session planning
Move scheduling into private text messages so the front desk no longer sees the booking
Decline the invitation and keep contact on the clinic channel used for scheduling
Accept dinner after closing the file so the personal plan and the work role look separate on paper

explanation: A date with a current client crosses the professional boundary and uses the power differential. Closing the chart so the dinner can happen, or moving contact to a private phone, does not end that imbalance. Appointment contact stays on the professional channel.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a nonclinical topic with a safe second relationship; dinner with a current client still blurs the boundary.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses convenience with professionalism; private texting pulls the relationship out of the clinic setting.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a closed file with the end of the power differential; paperwork does not make dating this client ethical.

prompt: A client proposes that the therapist invest personal money in the client's startup and continue weekly bodywork.

options.text: Invest and continue the sessions because adults may keep outside contact without an ethics question
Invest and continue the sessions because a consent checkbox clears the financial conflict from the business deal
Decline the investment while sessions continue so a money tie does not steer the plan
Accept the investment and add a medical diagnosis of the client's stress to the business advice

explanation: A business investment in a current client's company is a dual relationship that can bias the treatment plan toward protecting the investment. Ordinary adult contact is not the issue, and a checkbox does not remove the conflict. Diagnosing stress as part of the deal also leaves massage scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses ordinary adult contact with a financial stake in the client's business; the investment can bias care.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a consent checkbox with the absence of conflict; permission does not keep money from steering the plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a business deal with clinical scope; adding a medical diagnosis moves outside massage practice.

prompt: A runner asks the therapist to decide whether a painful calf lump is a clot and whether the race is safe.

options.text: Name the clot or rule it out, then clear the race if the tissue feels ordinary under the hands during palpation
Clear the race without naming a disease, because advice about sports readiness sits inside massage work
Avoid naming a disease, do not massage the painful calf, and refer the runner to a qualified clinician
Set a drug schedule for clotting and continue deep strokes over the painful calf

explanation: Massage therapists do not diagnose a clot or clear an athlete to compete. Until a clinician evaluates a painful calf lump that might be a clot, that calf is not massaged, because pressure can dislodge a thrombus. Prescribing a drug schedule is outside massage scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses palpation with a medical diagnosis; hands cannot confirm or exclude a clot or clear a race.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses general wellness talk with medical clearance; ruling a race safe is not a massage determination.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses massage with prescribing; a drug schedule is outside scope, and massage of a calf that may contain a clot can dislodge it.

prompt: In a crowded hallway a colleague asks aloud why a named client is here and what the diagnosis is.

options.text: Answer with the diagnosis so the colleague can help if the scheduled hour runs long
Repeat the diagnosis more quietly to people seated nearby so any rumor stays accurate
Move the talk to a private place and share details if that colleague is part of this client's care
Confirm the diagnosis on a public social page so visitors see that the clinic speaks openly about care

explanation: Health information is discussed in private and with people involved in that client's care, or when the client authorizes it. Helping the schedule, speaking more quietly, or looking transparent does not create a right to the diagnosis in a hallway.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses scheduling help with a treatment role; a long hour does not authorize a hallway diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses quieter speech with confidentiality; people seated nearby still should not hear the diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses marketing openness with consent; a public post of a named diagnosis is a privacy breach.

prompt: Gluteal work was approved at intake, and the therapist starts to pull the drape off both legs and the pelvis.

options.text: Remove the drape from the whole pelvis so the client can see that nothing is hidden while the gluteal muscles are treated
Work under the sheet without saying which region is uncovered or why the hands have moved
Uncover the gluteal area being treated, then cover it again before moving to another region
Skip draping for the pelvis because the intake form already mentioned gluteal work

explanation: Agreement to gluteal work allows the therapist to uncover that region while the gluteal cleft and genitals stay covered, and to tell the client which area is being touched. The drape goes back before the next region. An intake yes does not leave the pelvis and both legs bare.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses openness with draping; agreement to gluteal work does not mean the whole pelvis stays exposed.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a sheet on the body with informed contact; the client should know which region is being treated.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an intake yes with a reason to abandon draping; coverage is adjusted area by area during the session.

prompt: Oily fingers go back into an open cream jar between clients, and the hands have not been washed since the last session.

options.text: Wipe the hands on the used sheet and keep scooping from the same open jar for the person who is next
Rinse the fingertips when the next person asked for less time on the table today
Keep scooping from the open jar unless the intake form lists a skin infection
Wash the hands and dispense product so the bulk supply stays uncontaminated

explanation: Hands are washed between clients, and lubricant is dispensed so the bulk container is not contaminated by oily or unwashed fingers. Wiping on used linen, a brief rinse, or scooping from a shared jar unless a skin infection is listed leaves a path for cross-contamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a wipe on used linen with hand hygiene; the sheet is soiled and the jar stays contaminated.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a shorter session with a lower sanitation standard; session length does not change handwashing between clients.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses standard precautions with infection-only precautions; hands are washed and the bulk supply is protected between clients, not just after a disclosed skin infection.

prompt: The table is still set for a much taller coworker, so this therapist's shoulders hike and the wrists bend sharply on the hamstrings.

options.text: Stay on the toes and bend the wrists harder so the pressure feels stronger to the person lying on the table
Drop the chest onto the thigh and let body weight collapse through a rounded upper back
Raise the table higher so the shoulders can hang and the back can rest while the hands press
Reset the table height until the shoulders can drop and the wrists can stay near neutral

explanation: Table height is reset for the person doing the work. Dropped shoulders and a near-neutral wrist let the therapist deliver pressure without shrugging or collapsing. Rising onto the toes, hanging from a higher table, or folding onto the client loads the joints.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a harder wrist bend with effective pressure; the legs supply force while the wrist stays nearer neutral.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses collapsed weight with body mechanics; folding onto the client rounds the back and abandons a stable stance.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a higher table with less effort; a table that is too high hikes the shoulders instead of aligning them.

prompt: A client wants a copy of the massage notes for a physical therapist, and a neighbor in the lobby asks for the same packet.

options.text: Give the full packet to both people so the neighbor can help the client remember the home instructions after they leave
Refuse the client as well, on the view that notes must stay inside the clinic and cannot be copied
Pin the notes in the lobby so the client can photograph them without taking staff time
Release the copy to the client or a recipient the client authorizes, and withhold it from the neighbor

explanation: The client may receive their own treatment notes or direct that they go to another provider. A neighbor has no authorization, even when offering to help. Posting notes in the lobby exposes them to everyone there. Keeping the chart from the client is not what confidentiality requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a helpful neighbor with an authorized recipient; help with instructions does not permit disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses secure storage with a ban on release; the client can receive a copy of their own notes.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses convenience with confidentiality; a lobby posting lets unrelated people read the record.

prompt: An expensive gift and a weekend trip are offered, with a request that future sessions go easier on tender areas.

options.text: Accept the trip and lighten the work so the client feels repaid for the generosity
Accept the gift and describe it to other clients so the clinic appears popular, trusted, and worth booking again
Refuse the gift loudly and shame the client for raising it in the middle of the session
Decline gifts that pressure clinical choices and keep the plan tied to the assessment

explanation: Gifts tied to changing the treatment plan exploit the relationship. The work should follow assessment and consent, not a reward. The therapist can decline without shaming the client. Telling other clients about the gift also discloses a private exchange.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses generosity with a reason to alter care; easing the work as a reward lets the gift steer the plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a flattering story with professionalism; describing the gift to other clients discloses a private exchange.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a firm boundary with humiliation; the gift can be declined without shaming the client.

prompt: A race bib and a photo of the client's shoes are ready to post beside a note about today's plantar pain.

options.text: Publish the bib and the pain complaint because the client's face is outside the photo frame and therefore unnamed
Publish the story after the client's coach, a personal friend, says the post is welcome
Publish the first name and workplace but crop the bib so the image feels anonymous
Hold the post unless the client gives specific consent for that identifying story

explanation: A bib number, shoes, first name, workplace, or pain complaint can identify a client even when the face is absent. Consent to treatment is not consent to a public story. A coach who is the therapist's friend cannot authorize the post.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a cropped face with anonymity; a race bib and a pain complaint can still identify the client.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a friend's approval with the client's consent; the coach does not control that health information.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses removing the bib with anonymity; a first name plus a workplace can still identify the person.

prompt: The chart calls the client dramatic and noncompliant after the client stopped a stroke that hurt.

options.text: Leave the judgment in the chart because blunt wording protects the therapist if a later dispute questions the session
Delete the entire chart so there is no record that the stroke was painful or was stopped
Replace the entry with a promise that the next visit will leave the client free of pain
Rewrite the entry with observable facts, including that the client asked for the stroke to stop

explanation: Records describe what was observed and what the client reported or requested. Labels such as dramatic or noncompliant judge the person instead of documenting the event. Deleting the chart hides care, and a promise of a pain-free result is not an objective note.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a judgmental label with protection; observable facts, not character comments, belong in the chart.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses deletion with accuracy; removing the chart destroys the record of what occurred in the session.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a guarantee with documentation; promising a pain-free visit is not an observable finding.
